prompt: The passage uses the building analogy to illustrate which principle about the mind?

options.text: Both require regular use to prevent deterioration
Both must be built on a solid foundation
Both take longer to construct than to destroy
Both need periodic repair by an expert

explanation: Ecclesiastes 10:18 heads the chapter, and the gloss is: any building not put to use soon begins to run down, and runs down FASTER than one fully in use. In like manner, your mind will run down if not put to use.

why.a: Correct. Disuse, not age or damage, is what the analogy is about, on both sides of it.
why.b: Wrong. Foundations are a natural building metaphor but not the one drawn here.
why.c: Wrong. Speed of construction is not the comparison; the book's only speed claim is that an unused building runs down faster than a used one.
why.d: Wrong. Outside repair is not the remedy offered. The remedy is USE, by the owner.

prompt: Which scripture heads the chapter on the functions of the mind?

options.text: Ecclesiastes 10:18
Proverbs 4:23
Ecclesiastes 4:9
Hebrews 5:14

explanation: Ecclesiastes 10:18: 'By much slothfulness the building decayeth; and through idleness of the hands the house droppeth through.' Slothfulness and idleness are the two causes named.

why.a: Correct. This is the epigraph of the functions chapter, and it supplies the building image used immediately after.
why.b: Wrong. Proverbs 4:23 heads Chapter 1.
why.c: Wrong. Ecclesiastes 4:9 is 'Two are better than one', quoted later in this same chapter under understanding, which makes it a tempting near miss.
why.d: Wrong. Hebrews 5:14 heads Chapter 8 on exercising the mind.

prompt: What are the four major functions of the mind outlined in the passage?

options.text: Learning, understanding, reasoning and imagination
Learning, knowledge, understanding and wisdom
Knowledge, meditation, reasoning and imagination
Thinking, believing, remembering and deciding

explanation: The chapter names four and repeats them at its close: 'these functions learning, understanding, reasoning, and imagination'. Knowledge and meditation are discussed inside the chapter, but they are not among the four.

why.a: Correct. These are the four, in the order the chapter both introduces and summarises them.
why.b: Wrong, and it is the strongest trap. Knowledge IS discussed at length, but as what learning culminates in, and wisdom belongs to Chapter 4. Neither is one of the four functions.
why.c: Wrong. Meditation is presented as what PROCESSES knowledge into understanding, not as a function in its own right in this list.
why.d: Wrong. These are generic mental verbs the chapter does not use as its headings.

prompt: What does the passage say the mind is able to do under the function of learning?

options.text: Acquire and store information, making it available for use when required
Judge between competing claims without evidence
Receive revelation directly without study
Retain everything it is exposed to permanently

explanation: 'Learning takes place in the mind. The mind is able to acquire and store information, making it available for use when it is required.' Three verbs: acquire, store, make available.

why.a: Correct. Acquire, store and make available on demand are the three capabilities named.
why.b: Wrong. Judging belongs to reasoning, which is a separate function with its own section.
why.c: Wrong. Revelation without study is precisely what the book denies, insisting that even Daniel had to consult books.
why.d: Wrong. No claim of perfect retention is made; on the contrary the mind runs down without use.

prompt: Which of the following statements reflects Dr. T. L. Osborn's view as quoted in the passage?

options.text: When you stop learning, you start dying
When you stop learning, you're old, whether at 20 or 80
Make your brain work; it will sweat, but make it work
If the Spirit does not move me, I'll move the Spirit

explanation: T. L. Osborn is quoted twice in the book with this line, in Chapter 2 and again in Chapter 8. He is also quoted in Chapter 9 saying 'Every time you sin, something dies in you.'

why.a: Correct. This is Osborn's line, and the author says he totally agrees with it.
why.b: Wrong. That is Abraham Lincoln, quoted in the very next sentence, which is exactly why these two get confused.
why.c: Wrong. That is E. W. Kenyon, from his book Signposts On The Road to Success, quoted at the end of Chapter 8.
why.d: Wrong. That is Smith Wigglesworth, quoted in Chapter 6 on generating inspiration.

prompt: According to the passage, what did Abraham Lincoln say about learning and age?

options.text: When you stop learning, you're old, whether at 20 or 80
When you stop learning, you start dying
A man is never too old to begin again
Learning is the only thing the mind never tires of

explanation: The two ages are 20 and 80. Chapter 8 returns to him: anyone who stops learning is old, whether he is 80 years old or 20, and the greatest thing in life is to keep your mind young.

why.a: Correct. Lincoln's line names the two ages 20 and 80, and it is quoted twice in the book.
why.b: Wrong. That is T. L. Osborn, quoted immediately before Lincoln in the same paragraph.
why.c: Wrong. A plausible saying that is not in the book.
why.d: Wrong. The book says the opposite about an unused mind, which runs down.

prompt: What is the primary consequence of failing to engage in continuous learning according to the provided perspective?

options.text: A decline in both mental and physical vitality
A loss of respect among one's peers
A gradual loss of religious faith
An inability to hold a steady job

explanation: The chain is explicit: if your mind is not put to proper use your body soon begins to age, and people start ageing FROM THE MIND, not the body. Conversely, keeping the mind young will youngen your body.

why.a: Correct. Both are named, and the mental decline is said to cause the physical one.
why.b: Wrong. Peer respect is not the consequence discussed here.
why.c: Wrong. Loss of faith is not part of this argument.
why.d: Wrong. Employability appears in the mad man illustration of Chapter 1, not here.

prompt: According to the passage, what is the largest room in the world?

options.text: The room for improvement
The room of the imagination
The room of God's grace
The room a man makes for counsel

explanation: 'The largest room in the world, we are told, is the room for improvement.' It is offered as a reason to stay open to learn and conscious of the need to be current.

why.a: Correct. The pun on room is the whole saying, and the book attributes it vaguely with 'we are told'.
why.b: Wrong. Imagination is a function of the mind here, not the subject of this saying.
why.c: Wrong. Grace is required for inspiration in Chapter 6, but it is not this proverb.
why.d: Wrong. Counsel has its own section in Chapter 8 and is unrelated to this line.

prompt: Which individual is highlighted as a wise learner who, despite mastery over astrologers and magicians, continued to learn?

options.text: Daniel
Solomon
Joseph
Paul

explanation: Daniel, the wisest man in his time, was master of astrologers, magicians, Chaldeans and soothsayers, yet Daniel 9:2 records 'I Daniel understood by books...'. Being master over them did not excuse him from reading.

why.a: Correct. Daniel is the one whose mastery over astrologers and magicians is set against his continued study of books.
why.b: Wrong. Solomon is the wisdom figure of Chapters 4, 5 and 8, but he is not the one who mastered the astrologers, and his story here ends in loss.
why.c: Wrong. Joseph carries divine wisdom and interprets dreams, but the mastery over magicians and the books belong to Daniel.
why.d: Wrong. Paul is the other great learner in this same passage, but his mark is writing half the New Testament and still carrying books, not ruling over magicians.

prompt: Which scripture is quoted as "I Daniel understood by books..."?

options.text: Daniel 9:2
Daniel 1:17
Daniel 5:14
Daniel 2:30

explanation: Daniel 9:2 is the books verse, cited in Chapter 2 and again in Chapter 8 under research. The other three Daniel citations do different jobs.

why.a: Correct. Daniel 9:2 is the one about understanding by books.
why.b: Wrong. Daniel 1:17 is God GIVING the four children knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom, which is the gift, not the study.
why.c: Wrong. Daniel 5:14 is Belshazzar telling Daniel that the spirit of the gods is in him.
why.d: Wrong. Daniel 2:30 is Daniel's meekness, saying the secret was not revealed for any wisdom he had more than any living.

prompt: Which behavior is described as a common shortcoming of individuals who stop learning after leaving school?

options.text: Reading only the introduction and conclusion of a book
Focusing exclusively on technical manuals rather than wisdom
Reading only authors who agree with them
Buying books they never open at all

explanation: 'All they do is to read the conclusion and probably the introduction, and then close the book.' Note the order as printed: the CONCLUSION first, then probably the introduction.

why.a: Correct. This is the specific behaviour named, and it is deliberately small and concrete.
why.b: Wrong. This sounds exactly like something the book would say, which is what makes it dangerous, but technical manuals are never mentioned anywhere.
why.c: Wrong. The book actually advises reading those several times ahead of you, but never diagnoses this failing.
why.d: Wrong. This is close to the separate rebuke about books neatly arranged on your shelf whose contents you do not know, but it is not the shortcoming attached to leaving school.

prompt: How many books is Anthony Robbins reported to have read in his high school days?
explanation: 700 books, ranging from Psychology to Philosophy and various other subjects. Chapter 8 confirms the figure by calling him 'the 700-in-one man'.

why.a: Correct. Seven hundred, and the nickname in Chapter 8 fixes it.
why.b: Wrong. Five hundred is a plausible round number the book does not use.
why.c: Wrong. A thousand is the number people misremember because it sounds like the bigger claim.
why.d: Wrong. Three hundred is the amount in naira the author was earning when he did not borrow, from a different story entirely.

prompt: What does the passage say Anthony Robbins became after finishing high school?

options.text: An instant celebrity, and now a consultant to IBM and Presidents of many developed countries
A university lecturer in psychology
A publisher of the books that had shaped him
A pastor with a large congregation

explanation: Two stages: while still in school his teachers began consulting him and he became a man of solutions; on finishing he was an instant celebrity; now he consults for IBM and heads of state.

why.a: Correct. IBM and Presidents of many developed countries are both named.
why.b: Wrong. Psychology is named only as one of the subjects he read, not as a post he held.
why.c: Wrong. Publishing is not mentioned in his story.
why.d: Wrong. The large congregation belongs to David Yonggi Cho in Chapter 8.

prompt: Which individual is credited with writing about half of the New Testament?

options.text: Paul
Peter
Luke
John

explanation: 'This man wrote about 50% of the New Testament, yet, he was still carrying books and notes about.' The point of the fact is the contrast: even the man who wrote half of it kept reading.

why.a: Correct. Paul is credited with about 50 per cent of the New Testament here.
why.b: Wrong. Peter appears in this same passage, but as the one who SAID something about Paul's wisdom in 2 Peter 3:15-16.
why.c: Wrong. Luke is never discussed in the book.
why.d: Wrong. John's gospel is quoted several times, but no authorship share is claimed for him.

prompt: In 2 Timothy 4:13, what did Paul ask Timothy to bring, and what did he mean by it?

options.text: The cloak, the books, and especially the parchments, meaning his notes
The scrolls of the prophets, meaning the Old Testament
His letters to the churches, meaning his collected writings
His tools, meaning the means of his trade

explanation: 'The cloak that I left at Troas with Carpus, when thou comest, bring with thee, and the books, but especially the parchments.' The author's gloss: 'He was talking about his notes.' Chapter 8 cites the same verse for Paul always having a notebook by him.

why.a: Correct. Cloak, books and especially the parchments, which the author reads as Paul's own notes.
why.b: Wrong. The prophets are not what the verse names, and the whole force of the example is that these were his personal working papers.
why.c: Wrong. His letters are not the referent; parchments here means notes he was still using.
why.d: Wrong. Tentmaking tools are not mentioned in this book.

prompt: What did Peter say about Paul, as quoted in the passage?

options.text: That Paul wrote according to the wisdom given unto him, and that some things in his letters are hard to be understood
That Paul was the least of the apostles
That Paul had been taught by the Holy Ghost rather than by men
That Paul laboured more abundantly than they all

explanation: 2 Peter 3:15-16 is quoted to establish Paul as one of the wisest men in his days. Chapter 4 cites the same verses again, for Peter acknowledging that Paul's wisdom was in a class of its own.

why.a: Correct. Both halves come from the quotation: the wisdom given unto him, and things hard to be understood.
why.b: Wrong. That is Paul's own description of himself elsewhere, not Peter's, and it is not quoted here.
why.c: Wrong. The book credits God with giving Paul wisdom, but this is not the sentence Peter is quoted saying.
why.d: Wrong. Another genuine Pauline phrase from elsewhere that this book does not use.

prompt: What point does the passage make by pairing Paul and Daniel at the end of the section on learning?

options.text: God gave each of them wisdom, yet each still had to learn and consult books
Both were given wisdom without any effort of their own
Both lost their wisdom through pride
Both were self-taught without any divine gift

explanation: 'It was God who gave Paul wisdom, but Paul had to keep his mind alive by learning. God gave Daniel wisdom, yet Daniel had to consult books in order to acquire understanding.' Gift plus effort, not gift instead of effort.

why.a: Correct. The two halves are held together, which is the whole argument of the section.
why.b: Wrong. This drops the second half, and the second half is the point.
why.c: Wrong. Losing wisdom to pride is Solomon and Ahitophel in Chapter 5, not Paul and Daniel, who are both listed among those who made it.
why.d: Wrong. This drops the first half. The book says plainly that God gave them both wisdom.

prompt: How does the passage define knowledge?

options.text: The sum or range of what has been perceived, discovered or learned, and the familiarity, awareness or understanding gained through experience or study
The correct application of what one has learned
Information that has been tested and proved true
What the Holy Spirit reveals directly to the spirit of a man

explanation: A two-part dictionary style definition, following the claim that learning culminates in knowledge and that knowledge is what you acquire in the process of learning.

why.a: Correct. Both halves are given, the sum or range of what has been perceived, and the familiarity gained through experience or study.
why.b: Wrong. That is the definition of WISDOM, given at the top of Chapter 4. Confusing the two is the classic error this book is built to prevent.
why.c: Wrong. Testing and proof are not part of the definition offered.
why.d: Wrong. Direct revelation is inspiration in Chapter 6, and knowledge here is explicitly acquired through learning.

prompt: Which biblical citation is used in the passage to illustrate that knowledge can set a person free?

options.text: John 8:32
Hosea 4:6
John 8:7
Proverbs 13:15

explanation: John 8:32: 'ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free.' It is cited again at the end of the section: learning guarantees liberty, John 8:32, and exploits, Daniel 11:32.

why.a: Correct. John 8:32 is the freedom verse, quoted for knowledge having the ability to set free.
why.b: Wrong. Hosea 4:6 is quoted in the very same paragraph, but for the opposite: my people are DESTROYED for lack of knowledge.
why.c: Wrong. John 8:7 is 'He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her', used in the reasoning section.
why.d: Wrong. Proverbs 13:15 is 'Good understanding giveth favour', which belongs to understanding rather than knowledge.

prompt: Which scripture is quoted as "My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge"?

options.text: Hosea 4:6
John 8:32
Isaiah 5:13
Proverbs 1:7

explanation: Hosea 4:6, quoted in full including the reason: because thou hast rejected knowledge, I will also reject thee, that thou shalt be no priest to me.

why.a: Correct. Hosea 4:6 is the lack of knowledge verse.
why.b: Wrong. John 8:32 is the freedom half of the same paragraph.
why.c: Wrong. Isaiah 5:13 genuinely speaks of captivity for lack of knowledge, which makes it a fair guess, but this book does not quote it.
why.d: Wrong. Proverbs 1:7 is the fear of the LORD being the beginning of knowledge, used in Chapter 4 and Chapter 9.

prompt: What does the passage say knowledge is, beyond the gathering of information?

options.text: Power, with the ability to set free
A responsibility that will be judged
A foundation on which faith is built
A possession that grows only when shared

explanation: 'From this we understand that knowledge is not just the art of gathering information, it is power. It has the ability to set free.'

why.a: Correct. Power, and specifically power to set free, following from John 8:32.
why.b: Wrong. Judgment is not in view in this passage.
why.c: Wrong. The book grounds belief in the mind, but it does not describe knowledge as faith's foundation here.
why.d: Wrong. Sharing is not the mechanism discussed.

prompt: Why does the passage claim that a mad person cannot benefit from classroom instruction?

options.text: Because his mind is out of use and cannot assimilate the information.
Because he refuses to submit to a teacher's authority.
Because he cannot remain seated long enough to learn.
Because no teacher is willing to instruct him.

explanation: 'You may force him to sit down, but you can't force anything into him, because his mind is out of use... his mind, which is the tool for acquiring knowledge, is out of use.' The mind is the principal tool in the learning process.

why.a: Correct. The mind is the tool for acquiring knowledge, and his is out of use, so nothing can be assimilated.
why.b: Wrong. Refusal implies a working will making a choice, which is not the diagnosis.
why.c: Wrong, and it is the near miss. The passage explicitly grants that you CAN force him to sit down; sitting is not the problem.
why.d: Wrong. Willingness to teach is never mentioned.

prompt: What did the author see when he visited Reverend Kenneth E. Hagin in Tulsa Oklahoma?

options.text: A new book by Dr. T. L. Osborn lying open on his table, which he was reading
A library of several thousand volumes
A wall of framed testimonies from his meetings
His personal study notes stacked beside his bed

explanation: The detail is precise and is the point: a man of Hagin's stature still reading, and reading another living teacher. It sits in a run of examples about people who never stopped learning.

why.a: Correct. A new book by T. L. Osborn, open on the table, being read.
why.b: Wrong. No library is described, and a big library would actually weaken the point, which is about active reading.
why.c: Wrong. Testimonies are not mentioned in this anecdote.
why.d: Wrong. Books by the bedside belong to David Yonggi Cho's wife in Chapter 8.

prompt: At what age was Oswald J. Smith still consulting his dictionary, as noted in the material?
explanation: Still consulting his dictionary at 93; he LIVED to 96. Both numbers appear in the same two sentences, so keep them apart: 93 is the dictionary, 96 is the lifespan.

why.a: Correct. Ninety-three is the age at which he was still consulting his dictionary.
why.b: Wrong. Ninety-six is how long he lived, given in the very next line as the consequence: 'No wonder he lived for 96 years!'
why.c: Wrong. Seventy-two is Norman Vincent Pearle's years as an ordained minister, in the paragraph immediately after.
why.d: Wrong. Eighty is one of the ages in Abraham Lincoln's saying about being old at 20 or 80.

prompt: What discovery is Oswald J. Smith quoted as making from his dictionary?

options.text: That there is a major difference between faith and trust
That there is a major difference between knowledge and understanding
That there is a major difference between hearing and listening
That there is a major difference between wisdom and cleverness

explanation: 'As I was going through my dictionary, I discovered there's a major difference between faith and trust.' The pair is faith and trust.

why.a: Correct. Faith and trust is the pair he names.
why.b: Wrong, and it is the trap, because knowledge against understanding IS a major distinction in this book, drawn at length in the very next section. It just is not Smith's.
why.c: Wrong. Hearing and listening is a plausible modern pairing the book never uses.
why.d: Wrong. Wisdom is graded into four levels in Chapter 4, but never against cleverness.

prompt: For how many years was Norman Vincent Pearle an ordained minister?

options.text: 72 years
64 years
40 years
96 years

explanation: 72 years an ordained minister. He is also the man who taught the author the power of positive thinking, in 1974.

why.a: Correct. Seventy-two years in ordained ministry.
why.b: Wrong. Sixty-four years is the unnamed man in Chapter 8 who has stayed on successfully in ministry that long.
why.c: Wrong. About forty years is how long David Yonggi Cho has been at it in Chapter 8.
why.d: Wrong. Ninety-six is Oswald J. Smith's lifespan, from the paragraph just before.

prompt: What did Norman Vincent Pearle teach the author, and in what year?

options.text: The power of positive thinking, in 1974
The discipline of daily meditation, in 1981
The principle of seedtime and harvest, in 1974
The power of positive confession, in 1960

explanation: 'Norman Vincent Pearle was a great teacher, who taught me the power of positive thinking in 1974.' The book carries few dates, so the ones it has are worth holding.

why.a: Correct. The power of positive thinking, dated 1974.
why.b: Wrong. May 1981 is when the author laid hold of his understanding of prosperity in Ghana, a different story in Chapter 7.
why.c: Wrong. Seedtime and harvest is the covenant named in Chapter 4, not something Pearle taught.
why.d: Wrong. 1960 is the year of the earlier Kenneth Hagin book on healing mentioned in Chapter 9.

prompt: Which metaphor does the passage use to describe the effect of actively using one's mind?

options.text: Every divine deposit multiplies with use
The mind is a garden that needs watering
The mind is a muscle that grows under load
The mind is a lamp that must be kept trimmed

explanation: Drawn from the parable of the talent: 'From the parable of the talent, we see that every divine deposit multiplies with use.' The line is repeated twice on the same page.

why.a: Correct. This is the book's own image, and it is banking language, not gardening: a DEPOSIT that multiplies as it is used.
why.b: Wrong, and this is the single most dangerous distractor in the whole book. It is a real and familiar metaphor, it fits the theme perfectly, and it appears nowhere in the text.
why.c: Wrong. Another true-sounding modern metaphor. The book's nearest idea is exercising the senses in Chapter 8, but it never calls the mind a muscle.
why.d: Wrong. The lamp image is biblical but is not applied to the mind here.

prompt: What warning does the passage give with the figure of the local champion?

options.text: Do not die saying your shop is the biggest on your street when your street is an obscure place in an unknown area
Do not compare your business with those of your neighbours
Do not expand faster than your understanding allows
Do not take pride in a business built by dishonest means

explanation: The rebuke is about the SCALE of your reference frame. The remedy given is reading biographies of successful Christian businessmen so your business comes out of obscurity into the limelight.

why.a: Correct. The shop, the street and the unknown area are all in the sentence, and the point is that a small yardstick produces a small life.
why.b: Wrong. Comparison is an obstacle in Chapter 9, but this passage is about the size of your ambition, not about comparing.
why.c: Wrong. The book urges more expansion, not less.
why.d: Wrong. Dishonesty is dealt with under sin in Chapter 9 and is not this warning.

prompt: Why does the author say he always reads books by those who are several times ahead of him?

options.text: So that he can see his smallness and be determined to go forward
So that he can correct the errors in his own books
So that he can recommend them to his congregation
So that he can avoid repeating what others have already said

explanation: 'I always read books of those who are several times ahead of me, so that I can see my smallness and be determined to go forward.' He adds that he reads everything he can lay his hands on, to see if his brain can develop yet a little more.

why.a: Correct. Seeing his own smallness is the stated reason, and it produces determination rather than discouragement.
why.b: Wrong. He does say he keeps learning things he did not know when writing his own books, but that is a different sentence and not about correction.
why.c: Wrong. Recommending to others is not the motive given here.
why.d: Wrong. Originality is not the concern in this passage.

prompt: The passage says learning guarantees two things. Which pair, with their citations?

options.text: Liberty, from John 8:32, and exploits, from Daniel 11:32
Wisdom, from James 1:5, and understanding, from Job 32:8
Liberty, from Galatians 5:1, and dominion, from Genesis 1:28
Favour, from Proverbs 13:15, and peace, from Romans 8:6

explanation: 'Learning guarantees liberty (Jn. 8:32) and exploits (Dan. 11:32).' Daniel 11:32 is the verse behind the book's very title, about the people that do know their God being strong and doing exploits.

why.a: Correct. Liberty and exploits, cited to John 8:32 and Daniel 11:32.
why.b: Wrong. Both verses are used in the book, James 1:5 in Chapter 8 and Job 32:8 in Chapter 6, but neither is attached to this claim.
why.c: Wrong. Neither Galatians 5:1 nor Genesis 1:28 is quoted anywhere in this book.
why.d: Wrong. Both are genuine citations elsewhere in the book, which is what makes this tempting, but they are not what learning is said to guarantee.

prompt: On what condition does the passage say God has no problem dropping His deposit in you?

options.text: If you can convince God that you will not waste it
If you have first proved faithful in small things
If you ask for it in faith without doubting
If you are willing to give it away to others

explanation: 'If you can convince God that you will not waste it, God has no problem dropping His deposit in you.' It follows the prayer asking not to make God regret His rich deposits.

why.a: Correct. Not wasting it is the condition, matching the prayer just before about God not regretting His deposits.
why.b: Wrong. Faithfulness in little is a real biblical principle but not the condition stated here.
why.c: Wrong. That is the language of James 1:5, which the book uses in Chapter 8 for a different purpose.
why.d: Wrong. Giving is discussed under prosperity in Chapter 4, not as the condition for this deposit.

prompt: Complete the line from the parable of the talent: "Every divine deposit {{1}} with use."
explanation: Multiplies, not increases or grows. The word matters because the metaphor is a deposit that compounds, taken from the parable of the talent.

prompt: Complete Dr. T. L. Osborn's line: "When you stop learning, you start {{1}}."
explanation: Dying, which is the strongest of the options and the reason the line is memorable. The book then explains it: people start ageing from the mind, not the body.

prompt: The passage says a building not put to use runs down more slowly than a building that is fully in use.

options.text: True
False

explanation: False, and the direction is the whole point: 'It runs down FASTER than a building that is fully in use.' Use preserves, disuse destroys.

why.true: Wrong. It reverses the comparison, which would make the analogy argue against exercising the mind.
why.false: Correct. The unused building runs down faster, which is why an unused mind runs down too.

prompt: Match each person to the fact the passage attaches to them.

pairs.right: Wrote about 50 per cent of the New Testament
Found reading a new T. L. Osborn book in his office

extraLabels: Pastors the largest congregation on earth
explanation: This cluster of names and numbers on a single page is the densest target in the book. The decoys are all real facts from elsewhere: 96 is Smith's lifespan rather than his dictionary age, the largest congregation is David Yonggi Cho, and gravity is Isaac Newton in Chapter 8.

topic: books you own but have not read
prompt: What rebuke does the passage give about the books on a reader's shelf?

options.text: You know the titles and authors, but you don't know the contents
You buy more than you can ever read
You keep them for display rather than lending them
You read them once and never return to them

explanation: 'You have some books, true; but they are just there, neatly arranged on your library shelf. You know the titles and authors, but you don't know the contents!'

why.a: Correct. Titles and authors against contents is the exact contrast drawn.
why.b: Wrong. Quantity is not the charge; the book elsewhere praises reading 700 of them.
why.c: Wrong. Lending is never mentioned.
why.d: Wrong, and it is the near miss, because the author does praise rereading, saying he reads the same passage for 20 years and still finds something new. But that is a different sentence.

prompt: What does the author say about the books he himself has written on wisdom?

options.text: He still consults books by other authors on the subject and keeps learning things he did not know when writing his own
He no longer needs to read on a subject once he has written on it
He revises them each time he learns something new
He wrote them entirely from inspiration without consulting any source

explanation: The admission is the point of the paragraph: having written on wisdom does not exempt him from reading on wisdom. It sets up the rebuke to those who have not read one whole book since leaving school.

why.a: Correct. He consults other authors with delight and learns what he did not know when he was writing.
why.b: Wrong. This is exactly the attitude the paragraph exists to refute.
why.c: Wrong. Revising his books is never mentioned.
why.d: Wrong, and it is the subtle trap. Chapter 6 does say he made discoveries not from any book, but here he says the opposite about wisdom: he keeps consulting others.

prompt: What does the passage say will happen to your body if you keep your mind young by putting it to proper use?

options.text: It will youngen your body
It will preserve your body from disease
It will make your body require less rest
It will keep your body at its present state

explanation: The coined verb is the giveaway: 'If you keep your mind young by putting it to proper use, it will youngen your body.' Chapter 2 later adds that putting the mind to maximum use will invigorate and revitalize your body.

why.a: Correct. Youngen is the author's own word, which is exactly why it is quotable.
why.b: Wrong. Freedom from sickness is claimed elsewhere as evidence of study, but it is not this sentence.
why.c: Wrong. Rest is never discussed.
why.d: Wrong. The claim is active reversal, not preservation of the status quo.

topic: the question to ask about your mind
prompt: What question does the passage say you should ask yourself to keep your mind in top form?

options.text: What are the fundamental functions of my mind, so I can keep it alive and not watch it run down?
What have I learned today that I did not know yesterday?
Whose mind do I most want mine to resemble?
What is God asking me to do with my mind this year?

explanation: The question sets up the entire chapter, because the answer to it is the four functions: learning, understanding, reasoning and imagination.

why.a: Correct. This is the question as printed, and it is what the rest of the chapter answers.
why.b: Wrong. A sensible learning habit, but not the question asked here.
why.c: Wrong. Chapter 7 does say you will start thinking like the authors you read, but that is not this question.
why.d: Wrong. Nothing about an annual calling appears in this passage.
